newsitem.title: UK: European gasoline sales to US rise with temperature.
newsitem.headline: European gasoline sales to US rise with temperature.

text.p: Northwest Europe shipped at least 200,000 to 300,000 tonnes of gasoline to the United States in the second half of April but traders were unsure if the strong level of exports heading into the 1996 driving season would be matched this year.

The open arbitrage and several refinery maintenance turnarounds, however, may help tighten the NWE market which is chronically pressured by a roughly 10 percent overcapacity in gasoline production to demand, they said.
At least several cargoes of cat gas were also shipped in the last few weeks to the States from the Mediterranean, tightening that market, traders said.

"The arb (from NWE to the U.S.) is just open but for May and June people are concerned if May will be as strong...It's a tricky call this year," said one trader at a major oil company who awaited direction from NYMEX unleaded futures.

"There are two schools of thought and I'm right down the middle," he said. "There are two camps and on the one side they see a boost because the U.S. needs extra (barrels) and the inventory levels are lower."
Traders said Conoco, British Petroleum, Shell and Fina were all noted sellers to the States.
Conoco, for one, has confirmed that its 180,000 barrel per day South Killingholme refinery in U.K. would undergo six weeks maintenance, which traders said would cut its exports.
"Everyone was moving cargoes," said a trader at a European oil company who expected a similar amount to move in the first half of May.

In April of last year European countries shipped 6.70 million barrels of finished gasoline, reformulated gasoline and blending components to the U.S., about 223,000 barrels per day, according to U.S. Energy Information Administration data.
In June 1996, Europe, led by the U.K., Spain, Portugal, France and the Netherlands, sent 4.85 million barrels or about 162,000 bpd over 30 days, EIA said.

The four to five 60,000 tonne cargoes of mostly premium unleaded gasoline, totalling 2.0 to 2.5 million barrels, were considered about average demand for the U.S., which normally buys a quarter of its gasoline imports from Europe.
"That's probably about right for the second half of April," a broker said, while noting March shipments were higher. "I'm unsure for May because it depends on the arb."

The exports across the Atlantic and recent buying by one Scandinavian oil company in the barge market buoyed cargo prices in the last two weeks and may steady prices heading into May, some traders said.
NWE premium unleaded cargoes have steadily fallen from a high near $223 cif to a low near $196 in mid-April before bouncing back to $203 by Thursday.
"Perhaps it's a bit tighter than it has been," the trader at the major said. "It has not tightened up just yet but we may get a few days into May and see that that is the case."
A rich crack spread near $5.00-$5.25 a barrel, however, has deterred some bullish traders.

In addition, Western Europe gasoline demand has been flat in the last few years. The EIA estimated that 1996 OECD Europe demand was static at 2.929 million barrels per day from 2.924 million bpd in 1995.
Demand in May and June of 1996 fell to 2.971 million bpd and 2.978 from 2.996 and 3.095 in 1995, respectively, according to the EIA.
